title: Vitamin D: the sunshine hormone that influences the whole body
summary: Long confined to bone strength, vitamin D acts more like a hormone, involved in the muscles, immunity, the brain and metabolism. Made by the skin in the sun, it can be lacking in people who live mostly indoors, even in sunny regions, and deficiencies become more common with age. Natural light, oily fish and, for some, supplementation under medical supervision help maintain good levels.

blocks.text: Among all the nutrients studied in the field of healthy aging, few attract as much interest as vitamin D. For many years, it was regarded essentially as a vitamin needed for strong bones. Today, researchers know that its role is much broader.

In reality, vitamin D acts more like a hormone than a simple vitamin. Once produced or absorbed by the body, it takes part in regulating a large number of biological functions involving the muscles, bones, immune system, brain and general metabolism. This discovery has profoundly changed the way doctors approach the prevention of aging.

When vitamin D levels are insufficient for long periods, several of the body’s systems can be affected. Conversely, adequate vitamin D status helps keep many structures essential to health and independence working properly.
The main distinctive feature of this vitamin lies in how it is produced. Unlike most nutrients, which come mainly from food, vitamin D is made by our skin under the action of the sun’s rays.

For thousands of years, this natural production was the main source of supply for human beings. However, living conditions have changed profoundly. Today, a large part of the population spends most of its time indoors.

Days are often spent in offices, shops, factories, schools or at home. People get around by car or on public transportation. Even leisure activities are sometimes becoming more and more sedentary. This shift has considerably reduced exposure to sunlight for many people. Paradoxically, it is now possible to live in a very sunny region and still have insufficient vitamin D.

Older people are particularly affected. As we age, the skin gradually becomes less efficient at producing this vitamin. As a result, the same sun exposure often generates less vitamin D at seventy than at thirty.

In addition, older people sometimes spend less time outdoors because of limited mobility, chronic illness or more sedentary habits. This combination of factors explains why deficiencies become more common with age.

The importance of vitamin D shows first in the skeleton. Bones are not inert structures. They are constantly renewed through a complex balance between breakdown and rebuilding. To carry out this work, the body needs calcium, but also vitamin D.

Without enough vitamin D, intestinal absorption of calcium decreases. The bones then gradually become more fragile. This fragility increases the risk of osteopenia, osteoporosis and fractures. In older people, the consequences of a fracture can be particularly serious. A temporary loss of mobility can sometimes lead to a lasting decline in independence. Maintaining your vitamin D status therefore indirectly helps preserve functional independence.

But the effects of this vitamin go well beyond the skeleton. The muscles also have vitamin D receptors. When intake is insufficient, some people experience more muscle weakness, fatigue or reduced physical performance. Conversely, adequate status helps support normal muscle function. This action becomes particularly important after fifty, a period when the gradual loss of muscle mass begins to accelerate.

Vitamin D is also involved in how the immune system works. Our body is exposed every day to bacteria, viruses and other external agents. The immune system must maintain a subtle balance between vigilance and control.

Researchers have observed that vitamin D takes part in this complex regulation. It obviously does not replace a balanced diet, sufficient sleep or other healthy lifestyle measures, but it is one of the many factors contributing to the body’s overall robustness.

The brain is also a particularly active area of research. Neurons, too, have receptors able to respond to vitamin D. Scientists are currently studying the potential links between adequate vitamin D status and the maintenance of cognitive function during aging. Although many mechanisms remain to be clarified, it is clear that this vitamin contributes to the biological environment needed for proper brain function.

Mood also seems to be influenced. Many people notice their spirits dropping during periods when exposure to natural light is reduced. The link between light, vitamin D, biological rhythm and psychological balance is now the subject of significant research.
In a comprehensive approach to healthy aging, it therefore makes sense to consider vitamin D as one of the many elements contributing to physical and mental well-being.
Fortunately, several strategies make it possible to maintain adequate levels.

items: Reasonable exposure to natural light is the first of these.

Walking outdoors, gardening, exercising in the open air or simply spending more time outside often offer several benefits at once: exposure to light, physical activity, less sedentary time and improved general well-being.
Diet also makes a contribution, even though it generally remains insufficient on its own. The main dietary sources include: oily fish; sardines; mackerel; herring; some eggs; some fortified foods.

blocks.text: For some people, particularly older adults or those with a confirmed deficiency, supplementation may be considered under medical supervision.

The goal is not to seek excessive doses but to maintain a physiological balance suited to the body’s needs. As is often the case in preventive medicine, the best strategy relies on consistency rather than excess.
Good vitamin D does not turn an unhealthy lifestyle into good health. On the other hand, it is one of the many pillars that allow the body to keep functioning efficiently over the years.
The sun does not only give us light. Through vitamin D, it also helps maintain our bones, our muscles, our brain and our general vitality.
Preserving this balance is a simple step that can contribute lastingly to the quality of aging.
Family Clinic advice

Try to enjoy natural light every day, even for a short time. A morning walk combines several benefits at once: physical activity, exposure to daylight, a lift in mood, cardiovascular upkeep and support for the natural production of vitamin D. More than a simple nutrient, vitamin D is an integral part of the body’s overall balance.
